items.title: backoff: fix a timer leak in RunF
items.body:
If the context is canceled when `RunF` is blocked on `f()` and `f()` returns `nil`, the timer is reset, but is never stopped after that since RunF returns when it goes back to the `for` loop.

Here is a fix that will help:
```
diff --git a/internal/backoff/backoff.go b/internal/backoff/backoff.go
index 1234567..abcdef0 100644
--- a/internal/backoff/backoff.go
+++ b/internal/backoff/backoff.go
@@ -86,16 +86,19 @@ var ErrResetBackoff = errors.New("reset backoff state")
 func RunF(ctx context.Context, f func() error, backoff func(int) time.Duration) {
 	attempt := 0
 	timer := time.NewTimer(0)
+	defer timer.Stop()
 	for ctx.Err() == nil {
 		select {
 		case <-timer.C:
 		case <-ctx.Done():
-			timer.Stop()
 			return
 		}
 
 		err := f()
+		if ctx.Err() != nil {
+			return
+		}
 		if errors.Is(err, ErrResetBackoff) {
 			timer.Reset(0)
 			attempt = 0
 			continue
```

But there are no tests for this package. As part of fixing this, we should add full test coverage for this package.

@dashpole: This affects the xDS client as well since it made a copy of this package.

items.title: backoff: fix a timer leak in RunF
items.body:
Fixes #9485

What was the problem: If the context is canceled while RunF is executing f, and f returns nil, RunF returns without stopping the timer, even though the timer has been reset (the timer remains active).
What was changed: As described in the diff in the issue. Added `defer timer.Stop()` and checked the context immediately after f before returning.
Tests: Since this package had no tests, I added a new file, `backoff_test.go`. In line with the issue's recommendation to cover the entire package with tests, coverage is 100%.
Exponential.Backoff: Upper limit, jitter range, and ensuring values do not go negative.
RunF: Stops on error, resets, cancellation before execution, cancellation while waiting, and cancellation while `f` is executing (the leak in this case).
Verified: `go test -race -cpu 1,4` and `./scripts/vet.sh` pass. If I remove the fix, the leak test fails.
I haven't touched the copy of this package in the xDS client, since the issue raises it separately.

Follow-up to #9513: the same RunF exists verbatim in the xds copy.

#9513 fixes internal/backoff/backoff.go. internal/xds/clients/internal/backoff/ carries a byte-identical copy of RunF with the same leak from #9485: ctx canceled while blocked in f(), f() returns nil, and the timer gets re-armed by Reset right before RunF falls out of the loop.

items.title: xds/backoff: fix timer leak in RunF upon context cancellation and exit
items.body:
When RunF executes its inner function f, cancelling the context or encountering an early return while f is running leaves the retry timer active in the runtime timer heap. Because RunF reset the timer before evaluating the context state, the armed timer was never stopped on exit paths where the loop terminated early or when f returned an error.

This change ensures the retry timer is always cleaned up via defer timer.Stop(), and adds an immediate context cancellation check after invoking f to prevent re-arming the timer when the context is already done. Full test coverage has been added for the xds client internal backoff package to verify timer cleanup, jitter boundaries, and exponential backoff behavior under concurrent cancellation. All 9 test cases in backoff_test.go pass cleanly under the race detector.

RELEASE NOTES: n/a

items.title: xdsclient: flush any unsent loads when the LRS stream is closed

labels.name: Area: xDS
labels.description: Includes everything xDS related, including LB policies used with xDS.

items.body:
The LRS implementation in the xDS client transport can be found here: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-go/blob/55d8783479c7cc1a72a435340432702a67d809aa/xds/internal/xdsclient/transport/loadreport.go#L47

The `ReportLoad()` API returns a cancel func which is plumbed all the way to the user of the `XDSClient` API here: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-go/blob/55d8783479c7cc1a72a435340432702a67d809aa/xds/internal/xdsclient/client.go#L56

The current implementation of this cancel function simply cancels the context passed to the LRS stream, which results in the stream getting closed. But what we really want is for unsent loads to be flushed on the stream before it is closed.

The xDS client transport spawns the `lrsRunner` goroutine https://github.com/grpc/grpc-go/blob/55d8783479c7cc1a72a435340432702a67d809aa/xds/internal/xdsclient/transport/loadreport.go#L95 which (in a backoff loop) sends the first LRS request, receives the first response and then calls `sendLoads` to periodically send out load reports https://github.com/grpc/grpc-go/blob/55d8783479c7cc1a72a435340432702a67d809aa/xds/internal/xdsclient/transport/loadreport.go#L153

What we want is for the cancel function to synchronize with `sendLoads` so that when the cancel function is invoked, it results in unsent loads being flushed before the stream context is cancelled.

items.title: xds/testutils: add fakeTransport for testing.
items.body:
This PR introduces `fakeTransport`, a deterministic transport layer designed to facilitate fuzz testing of the xDS client in `grpc-go`.

### Purpose
The `fakeTransport` decouples the xDS client from the actual network, allowing tests to simulate management server interactions without establishing real connections. This is a critical component for the upcoming google3-based xdsClient fuzzer, which requires a way to inject specific responses directly into the client.

### Design
This component implements the `clients.TransportBuilder`, `clients.Transport` and `clients.Stream` interfaces.

*  When the `xdsClient` attempts to create a stream, the `Builder` intercepts these calls. Instead of establishing a real connection, it returns a local `FakeTransport` object.
*   The `FakeStream` replaces the network socket. It exposes standard methods  (`Recv`, `Send`) for the xdsClient, and control hooks (`InjectResponse`, `ReadRequest`). Allows the fuzzer to drive the xdsclient's resource parsing by pushing `DiscoveryResponse` protos and inspecting `DiscoveryRequest` messages via buffered channels.

### Future Scope
While primarily added for fuzzing, this utility is placed in `internal/testutils` to allow that it can be used by standard unit and e2e tests in the future.
Reference: [go/grpc-go-xdsclient-fuzzing](http://goto.google.com/grpc-go-xdsclient-fuzzing)

Part of : #8749

items.title: rls: Update logic in the control channel connectivity state monitoring goroutine
items.body:
Currently this is what the RLS LB policy is currently doing:
- Create an RLS control channel: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-go/blob/7472d578b15f718cbe8ca0f5f5a3713093c47b03/balancer/rls/balancer.go#L362
-  Start a goroutine to monitor the connectivity state of the channel: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-go/blob/7472d578b15f718cbe8ca0f5f5a3713093c47b03/balancer/rls/control_channel.go#L95
- The goroutine waits for the channel to become READY: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-go/blob/7472d578b15f718cbe8ca0f5f5a3713093c47b03/balancer/rls/control_channel.go#L188
- The next time it becomes READY again, it reset backoffs: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-go/blob/7472d578b15f718cbe8ca0f5f5a3713093c47b03/balancer/rls/control_channel.go#L202

This was a wrong assumption that once we are READY and get back to READY, we should have gone through TRANSIENT_FAILURE.

What should it should actually do:
- When the state transitions to TRANSIENT_FAILURE, record that transition
- The next time it transitions to READY, reset the backoff timeouts in all cache entries. Specifically, this means that it will reset the backoff state and cancel the pending backoff timer.  

We should also update this test: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-go/blob/7472d578b15f718cbe8ca0f5f5a3713093c47b03/balancer/rls/balancer_test.go#L916 to ensure that a transition from READY to IDLE to READY does not result in backoff timeouts being reset.

items.title: credentials/google: make a non-blocking and context-aware call to fetch token.

labels.name: Type: Feature
labels.description: New features or improvements in behavior

labels.name: Area: xDS
labels.description: Includes everything xDS related, including LB policies used with xDS.

items.body:
This PR is a follow-up to [PR #9118](https://github.com/grpc/grpc-go/pull/9118), refactoring the newly added GCP Service Account Identity call credentials to fetch tokens asynchronously and pass a 60 sec context timeout.

Previously, if a valid token was not cached, GetRequestMetadata performed a blocking synchronous call to `creds.TokenProvider.Token(context.Background())`. This block occurred while holding the c.mu mutex lock, which blocked all other concurrent metadata retrievals. Additionally, the token fetch did not have a timeout and relies on the 15 sec timeout that metadata server works with.

This PR refactors the credential to:
* Run the token fetch in a background goroutine, releasing the mutex lock during the network call.
* Deduplicate concurrent fetches using a channel broadcast pattern.
* Allow waiting RPCs to unblock immediately if their context is canceled or expires.
* Bound the background fetch itself with a defensive 60-second timeout.

RELEASE NOTES: N/A

items.title: credentials: add `GcpServiceAccountIdentityCallCredentials` call credentials type (gRFC A83).

labels.name: Type: Feature
labels.description: New features or improvements in behavior

labels.name: Area: xDS
labels.description: Includes everything xDS related, including LB policies used with xDS.

items.body:
This PR implements `GcpServiceAccountIdentityCallCredentials`, a new call credentials type required by [gRFC A83: xDS GCP Authentication Filter](https://github.com/grpc/proposal/blob/master/A83-xds-gcp-authn-filter.md#call-credentials). This credential fetches and manages GCP Service Account Identity tokens for a given audience, allowing gRPC services running on GCP to authenticate RPCs.

**Implementation Details & gRFC Deviations**

The gRFC provides detailed specifications for how this credential should manually fetch tokens from the GCE metadata server, extract the exp field, and manually calculate refresh intervals (e.g., refreshing 30 seconds early).

However, we have decided to use google auth library to fetch the token.

In Go, the standard Google API authentication packages (golang.org/x/oauth2/google) only provide access tokens, which are fundamentally different from the identity tokens required here.

To properly fetch identity tokens, we have decided to use the officially supported Google Auth library for Go: `cloud.google.com/go/auth/credentials/idtoken`.

The library causes the following behavioral difference from gRFC.
* Hardcoded early expiry: The idtoken package has its own internal logic and hardcoded values for when to proactively refresh a token (currently, it expires tokens 5 minutes early, not 30 seconds early as suggested by the gRFC).
* Execution: We rely on idtoken.NewCredentials to handle the HTTP requests to the metadata server, extraction of the JWT, and cache invalidation.

Behavioral Guarantees Implemented:
* Handles fetching the token on-demand based on the provided audience.
* Ensures data-plane RPCs block concurrently while a single background network request fetches the token.
* Applies standard exponential backoff if the token fetch fails.
* Injects the authorization: Bearer <token> header into outbound metadata.

RELEASE NOTES: N/A

### What version of gRPC are you using?
client: v1.70.0, server: v1.61.1, v1.63.2, v1.66.0.

### What version of Go are you using (`go version`)?
go version go1.22.11 linux/amd64

### What operating system (Linux, Windows, …) and version?
several Linux versions, including: kernel 4.15.0-112-generic on Ubuntu

### What did you do?
gRPC client with a custom resolver (using `pick_first` LB), connecting to a multi-node server cluster. this codebase appeared to be working fine for about 6 years, up to and including gRPC v1.63.2 - or at least the issue below was never brought to our attention before. since upgrading to v1.70.0, the same code appears to _occasionally_ enter infinite loop calling the custom resolver's `ResolveNow()` method. the issue is non-deterministic, but has been observed 4-5 times in the past month, AFAICT - always on network transients (impaired connectivity to the gRPC servers cluster).

items.title: Resolver state is not updating during kubernetes rolling update
items.body:
### What version of gRPC are you using?
v1.72.2

### What version of Go are you using (`go version`)?
Go 1.23

### What operating system (Linux, Windows, …) and version?
Linux (alpine3.19)

### What did you do?
I am running a golang micro service architecture on kubernetes. I have a client and a server communicating internally in the k8s cluster via gRPC. 
The client is unable to successfully relay rpcs to the server whilst the server is undergoing a rolling update and for up to 30 seconds after the rolling update has been completed.
The server is exposed to the client through a k8s headless service, the client has the service name configured as  target (prefixed with dns:/// for the DNS resolver to be used) and is configured to load balance using round_robin.
The client starts the grpc connection using grpc.NewClient(target, g.dialOptions()...)

The issue I am now facing is that the resolver state only gets updated successfully aprox. 30s after the rolling update has completed. I am assuming this time is simply the minResolutionInterval of the DNS resolver. During these 30s all requests from client to server end in a "connection refused" error. 
From researching on the internet I had made the assumption that the resolver state would get updated on any error, but analyzing the gRPC debug logs seems to indicate that it only resolves state directly on the grpc client errors, or the underlying channels erroring and not e.g on rpc errors happening on said channels.

Is this working as intended?

Things I have tried to configure in and outside the gRPC client to change the behaviour:
- dns.SetMinResolutionInterval(1 * time.Second)
- Default Service Config with ->  healthCheckConfig
- Keepalive Params -> Time: 10s, Timout: 3s, PermitWithoutStream: true
- Retry Config -> PerRetryTimeout: 30s, WithMax: 10


I wrote a small test script orchestrating the kubernetes rolling update of server, monitoring the clients gRPC logs, as well as monitoring the k8s endpointslice. The client itself has a REST API which then in turn exeutes one rpc on the server. During the rolling update my test script uses said REST API on an interval.

items.title: xdsclient: new Transport interface and ADS stream implementation

labels.name: Type: Internal Cleanup
labels.description: Refactors, etc

items.body:
#a71-xds-fallback
#xdsclient-refactor

The existing structure of the xDS client is as follows:
- the xDS client has an `authority` type for each authority configuration in the bootstrap (ignoring authority sharing)
- each `authority` has a `Transport` which contains a `grpc.ClientConn` to the xDS management server
- the `Transport` type provides the following functionality
  - runs an ADS stream, and allows the authority to trigger a `DiscoveryRequest` to be sent
  - runs an LRS stream, and allows the authority to start the load reporting

The new structure for the xDS client will be as follows:
- the xDS client will have one `authority` type for each authority configuration in the bootstrap (even if the authority configuration are the same or have the same server configuration)
- the xDS client will own a bunch of `xdsChannel`s, one each for each server configuration specified in the bootstrap
- each `authority` will acquire references to one of more `xdsChannel` instances
- each `xdsChannel` will contain the following
  - a `Transport` to the xDS management server. This will be an interface allowing for non-grpc transports to be used.
  - an ADS stream instance that runs an ADS stream and supports resource subscription/unsubscription.
  - an LRS stream instance that runs an LRS stream and support starting and stopping the stream.

This PR introduces the following functionality:
- Defines the `Transport` interface and provides a gRPC transport implementation.
- An ADS stream implementation.

The current ADS implementation can be found in hhttps://github.com/grpc/grpc-go/blob/master/xds/internal/xdsclient/transport/transport.go, and this PR's implementation is heavily based off of it.

Subsequent PRs will add more functionality.

Addresses https://github.com/grpc/grpc-go/issues/6902

RELEASE NOTES: none

items.title: pickfirst: New pick first policy for dualstack

labels.name: Type: Feature
labels.description: New features or improvements in behavior

items.body:
This PR moves the pickfirst logic into the LB policy as mentioned in [A61](https://github.com/grpc/proposal/blob/master/A61-IPv4-IPv6-dualstack-backends.md#move-pick_first-logic-out-of-subchannel-javago).

## Background

In Java and Go, pick first logic is implemented within the subchannel itself instead of inside the load balancer unlike C-core.

We will take this opportunity to bring gRPC to a more uniform architecture across implementations and write a new pick first policy. This is important so that different implementations do not continue to diverge as more features are implemented.

This change will include creating a PickFirstLeafLoadBalancer which will contain the pick first logic, as well as redesigning some components such as backoffs and address updates. This will set us up nicely to implement Happy Eyeballs and use pick first as a universal leaf policy.

The new pick first policy is not used by default and can be set using an environment variable. A GitHub actions workflow is created to run the tests with the env var set. Code coverage is also calculated by running with and without the env var set.

This implementation is based on the [Java implementation](https://github.com/grpc/grpc-java/blob/70ae83288de6a712e905c0f97eebd5713ad01677/core/src/main/java/io/grpc/internal/PickFirstLeafLoadBalancer.java).

RELEASE NOTES:
- An experimental pick first LB policy is added which creates one subchannel per address. This is disabled by default until the Dualstack changes are completed.

items.title: rls: update picker synchronously upon receipt of configuration update
items.body:
https://github.com/grpc/grpc-go/issues/5469 recommends an audit of existing LB policies to ensure that they update their pickers synchronously upon receipt of a configuration update.

`rls` LB policy does not update its picker synchronously in one corner case.

- Configuration updates are handled here: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-go/blob/b4f7947184ed45e72283a37aeaf214e38c35bc63/balancer/rls/balancer.go#L252
- The LB policy inhibits picker updates until the new configuration is pushed to all child policies. See: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-go/blob/b4f7947184ed45e72283a37aeaf214e38c35bc63/balancer/rls/balancer.go#L270
- In a blocking fashion, it does the following
  - pushes updates to child policies
  - waits for picker updates from all the child policies
  - sends a new picker
  - See: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-go/blob/b4f7947184ed45e72283a37aeaf214e38c35bc63/balancer/rls/balancer.go#L293
- At the end of `UpdateClientConnState`, the LB policy handles any changes to the data cache size here: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-go/blob/b4f7947184ed45e72283a37aeaf214e38c35bc63/balancer/rls/balancer.go#L297
  - The return value from the resize operation is ignored here: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-go/blob/b4f7947184ed45e72283a37aeaf214e38c35bc63/balancer/rls/balancer.go#L306
  - The return value should not be ignored. Instead if any entry with a backoff timer was evicted, then it should result in a new picker being sent upwards.

Quoting this from the design:
```
When removing an entry whose backoff_time_ is in the future, the backoff timer 
will be cancelled.  Note that just like when the backoff timer fires normally, a new
 picker is returned to the channel, to force it to re-process any wait-for-ready RPCs
that may still be queued if we failed them while we were in backoff.
```

items.title: Wait for ready with "readiness timeout"

labels.name: Type: Feature
labels.description: New features or improvements in behavior

items.body:
### Use case(s) - what problem will this feature solve?

We have a long running stream (`rpc Stream(StreamRequest) returns (stream StreamResponse) {}`). On the client side we would like to open the stream and then have it open indefinitely. If a recoverable error happens, we would like to restart it. If a non-recoverable error happens, we would like to quit. 

### Proposed Solution

It would be great if the WaitForReady flag had an optional "readiness timeout": a timeout only for having the connection ready, not for the whole RPC.

### Alternatives Considered

#### Timeout in the retry config
``` json
{
  "methodConfig": [{
    "name": [{"service": "..."}],
    "waitForReady": true,
    "timeout": "10s",
  }]
}
```
The timeout in the above config unfortunately stops the stream even if it's ready (and flowing).

#### Stream context timeout
``` go
ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 3 * time.Second)
defer cancel()
stream, err := client.Stream(ctx, &streampb.StreamRequest{})
```
Same issue: this will cancel the stream after 3 seconds even if there were no errors at all.

#### Connection context timeout
``` go
// waitForReady is true in the retryConfig
ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 3 * time.Second)
defer cancel()
conn, err := grpc.DialContext(ctx, address, grpc.WithDefaultServiceConfig(retryConfig))
```
This will never timeout if the server is not available.

#### Timeout in a different goroutine
``` go
timeout := 3 * time.Second
timer := time.NewTimer(timeout)
errCh := make(chan error)
go func() {
  stream, err := client.Stream(ctx, &streampb.StreamRequest{})
  defer timer.Stop()
  if err != nil {
    errCh <- err
    return
  }
  errCh <- readStream(ctx, stream)
}()
go func() {
  <-timer.C
  errCh <- fmt.Errorf("stream timeout after %s", timeout)
}()
return <-errCh
```
This works as expected: if we manage to connect to the stream within 3 seconds, it will stream until `ctx` is canceled. If we don't, we return an error. The problem is that the error is not very helpful ("stream timeout after 3s"). We cannot use the stream returned by `client.Stream()`, because with wait for ready it never returns.

items.title: Correct way to perform a reconnect with gRPC client
items.body:
I have an application that successfully works with single GRPC server. We have implemented GRPC server to be running on multiple nodes for redundancy. Our client calls server every 2-3 seconds.
When we restart one of the nodes, client that was connected to that node loses connection, but regains it back almost immediate when it is up.
On the other hand if the node is down permanently, it takes between 6-15 min until client reconnects to different server.

What is the correct way to make gRPC client to reconnect in case of RPC failure?

Bellow is our current client connection implementation:

```
func dialConnection(connString string) *grpc.ClientConn {
	tlsCredentials := insecure.NewCredentials()
	ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), time.Second*time.Duration(5))
	defer cancel()
	conn, err := grpc.DialContext(ctx, connString,
		grpc.WithTransportCredentials(tlsCredentials),
		grpc.WithBlock())
	if err != nil {
		return nil
	}
	return conn
}
```

connection string will look like "grpcserver.company.com:50051" while DNS resolver will return IPs for all servers.

labels.name: Type: Behavior Change
labels.description: Behavior changes not categorized as bugs

items.body:
The xdsclient needed some modification to align to the Failure Mode Behavior specified in [A57](https://github.com/grpc/proposal/blob/master/A57-xds-client-failure-mode-behavior.md). This diff adds the following changes: 

1. Per A57, gRPC-Go should not use `wait_for_ready` while creating the ADS stream. This is because we depend on the stream to fail when the channel is in `TRANSIENT_FAILURE`, in order to obtain the status message for the connectivity failure.

1. Previously, the timer to watch resource was initialized when authority.watchResource() api was called. 

    Per A57
    > The timeout period should start as soon as both of the following are true:
    > 
    > The first message subscribing to the resource has been sent on the stream.
    > A connection has been established to the xDS server and the stream has been dispatched to the associated transport.
  
     In this change, the timer starts only when the transport signals back to the authority after a successful send().

1. A new resource watch state `watchStateRespRequested` to represent when the resource request has been sent by the transport
1. Add `OnSendHandler` to transport.Options to send updates from transport.

Fixes: #5753 

RELEASE NOTES:
* xdsclient/transport: stop using wait_for_ready dial option when creating ads stream + xdsclient/authority: watch resource timer starts after transport sends resource request

items.title: Callback for client-side connection errors

labels.name: Type: Feature
labels.description: New features or improvements in behavior

items.body:
Hi, 

I'm trying to catch as many connection errors as possible when dialing from grpc client to grpc server. I am already using the `grpc.WithReturnConnectionError()` dial option to get the latest connection error. This doesn't help for me, because I am using a **clustered** grpc server and I need more than the latest error, because this will only return the error of the last cluster node. And even if the grpc client successfully connects to a cluster node, I want to know, if any of the previous connection establishments failed.

I am aware of the `GRPC_GO_LOG_VERBOSITY_LEVEL=99` and `GRPC_GO_LOG_SEVERITY_LEVEL=info` environment variables, but I want to build a custom error management.

I am also aware of the `grpc.WithContextDialer(...)` dial option, but this only helps to detect DNS and TCP issues, not TLS. And even with a custom `grpc.WithTransportCredentials(...)` I was not able to catch 100% of possible dial errors.

### Proposed Solution

There is already a function `func (cc *ClientConn) updateConnectionError(err error) {...}` that stores the latest connection error. This function could be extended with an optional callback that will be called on connection errors. The callback could then be passed as dial option, e.g. `grpc.WithOnConnectionError(func(addr resolver.Address, err error) {...})`.

items.title: Connection age context

labels.name: Type: Feature
labels.description: New features or improvements in behavior

items.body:
### Use case(s) - what problem will this feature solve?

I have a server that handles long running bi-directional streams. Clients establishes a connection and then server may eventually have something to reply with. The request may be open for minutes, hours, days. In the middle there is a load balancer so I have to ensure the connection is closed before the timeout setting on the load balancer, otherwise it aborts the connection. To do that server has max connection age set to a number and in addition to that on each request code starts a timing out context. Once it times out, the server just returns `nil` from the handler, closing the connection cleanly. Client sees `io.EOF` and reconnects immediatelly, likely using a different TCP connection.

The problem is that sometimes the server has multiple things to reply with over a period of time that is smaller than max connection age. In this case the underlying TCP connection is reused and my timeout context only signals "done" when it's too late and the max connection age grace has also expired. Actually, the request's context signals sooner than my own context. The client gets an error (`rpc error: code = Unavailable desc = closing transport due to: connection error: desc = "error reading from server: EOF", received prior goaway: code: NO_ERROR, debug data:`) rather than `io.EOF`.

### Proposed Solution

Let the request handler know how much time it can occupy the connection for without breaching the max connection age. Ideally it's a context that is canceled when max connection age duration elapses.

Request context is a different thing. It's "done" when max connection age grace duration elapses and the connection is aborted. Even if handler returns `nil`, client gets an error.

### Alternatives Considered

For now I have came up with a workaround - max poll duration that a handler can wait for an event is just a little under 50% of the max connection age. And then max connection age for gRPC is set to 35% of the max connection age for the load balancer. This way even if some time is "consumed" by the "fast" requests, a long request that starts right before 
max connection age for gRPC expires, can still run for ~50% of time and end without breaching the overall max connection age of the load balancer. 35% is because it's 35% +/- 10% jitter - must be under 50%.

The above works but it's wasteful as connections could be sitting idle for much longer. Instead, both server and client have to do work to re-establish the network and logic connection/etc.

### Additional Context

Fix/workaround is here https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/cluster-integration/gitlab-agent/-/merge_requests/424, perhaps it can help understand the issue I'm having. Thank you.

items.body:
Please answer these questions before submitting your issue.

### What version of gRPC are you using?
grpc-go v1.12.0

### What version of Go are you using (`go version`)?
go1.10.2 darwin/amd64

### What operating system (Linux, Windows, …) and version?
Debian GNU/Linux 8.11 (jessie)

### What did you do?
We stream messages to the server using a normal stream. We establish the connection at system start, and cache a stream stream until either the client or server is shut down.

Establish connection:
```
    conn, err := grpc.Dial(addr,
        grpc.WithInsecure(),
        grpc.WithBackoffMaxDelay(time.Millisecond*500),
        grpc.WithKeepaliveParams(keepalive.ClientParameters{
            Time:                time.Millisecond * 500,
            Timeout:             time.Second * 2,
            PermitWithoutStream: true,
        }),
        grpc.WithDefaultCallOptions(
            grpc.MaxCallSendMsgSize(1024*1024),
            grpc.MaxCallRecvMsgSize(1024*1024),
            grpc.FailFast(true),
        ),
    )
```

Proto def:
`rpc Raft(stream RaftRequest) returns (RaftReply) {}`

Send msg:
```
    func (t *transport) StreamRaftMsg(msg *sifpb.RaftRequest) error {
        if t.raftClient == nil {
            rc, err := t.Raft(context.Background())
            if err != nil {
                return err
            }
            t.raftClient = rc
        }

        if err := t.raftClient.Send(msg); err != nil {
            t.closeStream()
            t.raftClient = nil
            return err
        }
        return nil
    }
```

### What did you expect to see?
Our expectation was that all requests to `StreamRaftMsg` would become unblocking,  when the connection becomes unhealthy - either by pings failing or the server shutting down.

We also have a number of unary rpc calls which we expect to either cancel already running requests or fail instantly when called while connection is down.

### What did you see instead?
If we take down the server everything works as we intended. Everything fails instantly. However if we introduce a partitioning, like a firewall rule, all rpc requests and stream creation calls become blocking or block until their context times out.

Example firewall rule applied on the server:
`sudo iptables -A OUTPUT -d <client-hostname> -j DROP`

These symptoms happen in production when a server become unstable. I've been able to work around this by buffering outgoing requests and have a separate go routine drain that buffer. The go routine would then handle the blocking. This is not a great solution. 

It is perfectly fine for us to drop packages when the connection is down. It is however crucial that all requests are fail fast if either the internal grpc buffer is full or the connection becomes unhealthy.

What are your suggestions for getting these properties?

It might also make sense to consider REFUSED_STREAM failures as retryable.
